hook.text: A model wants numbers, not lists of words.

unit.text: So this unit turns text into features: rows of numbers a program can learn from.

menu.text: But first, a choice. The cleaning steps are a menu, not a recipe.

steps.text: You'll nearly always tokenize. After that, every step is a question. Lowercase? Drop stopwords? Stem or lemmatize? Add n-grams?

test.text: And each one has the same test. Does what this step throws away matter to your task? If it's noise, drop it. If it's signal, keep it.

review.text: Take one review. The plot was not good, but the acting was brilliant.

topic.text: A topic pipeline drops every stopword. The words not and but are both on NLTK's list, so what's left is plot, good, acting, brilliant.

about.text: That's fine for what the review is about. But read it for feeling, and it now just says good.

sentiment.text: A sentiment pipeline keeps the negations, and adds word pairs, so not good survives as a unit.

tasks.text: Every task chooses differently. Search wants stems. Topics want real words, so lemmas. Sentiment keeps its stopwords.

author.text: And to tell who wrote a text, the stopwords are the signal itself.

ablate.text: So don't guess. Change one step at a time, and measure on your own task. That's called an ablation.

default.text: A safe default: tokenize, lowercase, and keep the stopwords until a measurement says to drop them.

count-in.text: With the tokens chosen, the next job is to count them.

bag.text: The simplest way is a bag of words. Tip a document's words into a bag and shake it. You keep which words, and how many times, but not their order.

vocab.text: Take three tiny documents. First, build a vocabulary: every distinct word, sorted. Here, that's nine.

rows.text: Then give each document a row, with one column per word. The first document has the word the twice, and cat, mat, on and sat once each.

matrix.text: That's a document-term matrix. Every row has the same nine columns, so rows can be compared, added up, and handed to a classifier.

binary.text: Sometimes all that matters is whether a word is there. This spam says free three times.

vectors.text: The count vector keeps the three. The binary vector just marks a one, for present.

order.text: The bag has blind spots. Dog bites man and man bites dog make exactly the same bag.

sparse.text: Real vocabularies run to tens of thousands of words, so almost every cell is zero.

meaning.text: And great and excellent are just two unrelated columns. The bag knows nothing about meaning.

common-in.text: One weakness has a neat fix, though: the most common words get the biggest counts, and say the least.

counts.text: Here are three new documents: a cat on a mat, a dog in a park, a comet in the sky. By raw count, the word the leads every row, with two.

same.text: But a column that's the same in every row can't tell the documents apart.

idf.text: TF-IDF weighs each word by how telling it is. Start with inverse document frequency: divide the number of documents by how many contain the word, then take the natural log.

idf-the.text: The word the is in all three. Three over three is one, and the log of one is zero.

idf-cat.text: Cat is in just one, so it gets the log of three, about one point one.

tf.text: Now multiply by term frequency, each word's share of its document. Cat is one word in six, so it scores about zero point one eight.

flip.text: The word the is two in six, times zero. The column that led every row drops to zero.

tie.text: At the top of the first document, cat, mat, on and sat tie. On says nothing about cats, but it's just as rare, and rarity is all IDF can see.

rule.text: So TF-IDF rewards words that are frequent here and rare elsewhere, with no stopword list at all.

sklearn.text: One caution: that's the textbook formula. Scikit-learn's default smooths it and adds one, so the word the never reaches zero. On these three documents, it even stays on top.

decide-in.text: Counts and weights describe a text. The last step makes a call on one: is it positive, or negative?

lexicon.text: The simplest sentiment classifier is two word lists: seven positive words, and seven negative.

score.text: Add one for each positive word, take one away for each negative word, and read the sign.

naive.text: I love this movie: positive. This film is terrible: negative. It is not good...

wrong.text: positive. The counter sees good, and never reads the not.

blind.text: Counting words one at a time is a bag of words, so it's blind to order, too.

flag.text: The fix is one flag. A negation like not, no or never switches it on, and the next sentiment word flips its sign.

reset.text: A comma, a full stop, or the word but switches it off again, so a not can't reach into the next clause.

fixed.text: Now, it is not good comes out negative. And this is not bad at all comes out positive.

mixed.text: The plot was good but the acting was awful? Plus one, minus one... neutral.

limits.text: Rules have ceilings. Take sarcasm: oh great, another delay scores positive, because the words can't see the wink.

context.text: Context, too: unpredictable is bad in brakes and good in a thriller. And a word missing from the lists counts for nothing.

baseline.text: Still, a rule-based baseline is worth building first. It's fast, it needs no training data, and it gives you a score to beat.

learn.text: When it falls short, models learn from labeled examples. But they still tokenize, clean and count, just like this unit did.

next.text: And many of these ideas are much older than they look. IDF dates from nineteen seventy-two, and counting word pairs from nineteen forty-eight.
